strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: exploiting slot annotations to learn useful representations of task-oriented utterances. Template augmentation and joint utterance–template contrastive learning form a coherent, practical approach.

The reported results provide meaningful evidence of benefit across five datasets. In Table 3, TaDSE with MLP achieves 83.87 average accuracy versus 81.82 for DSE. Including baselines trained on the augmented data helps distinguish the proposed method from simply supplying more examples.

The component ablations are useful: Table 5 shows improvements from adding template and pairwise losses across three datasets. The investigation of augmentation strength and explicit discussion of noisy CLINC150 entities also help characterize when the approach works.
weaknesses: Important reproducibility and comparison details remain unresolved. Appendix B supplies several training settings but omits contrastive temperatures and sufficient specification of pooling and the template MLP. It states that evaluation uses full utterance/template training representations without clearly specifying the reference collection for each baseline, including whether synthetic utterances and templates are included equally. Consequently, gains cannot be confidently attributed entirely to encoder quality. Code is only promised.

The negative-pair construction conflicts with the many-to-one relationship motivating the method. In Equation 3, another utterance generated from the same template becomes a negative whenever it occurs in the batch. Comparing distinct utterances does not ensure that they are incorrect template matches. The paper should specify whether sampling excludes these collisions, quantify their frequency, or evaluate a loss that recognizes multiple valid positives.

The geometric analysis contains a concrete inconsistency requiring resolution. Figure 8 reports uniformity around −12 to −10. For unit-normalized embeddings, Equation 6 cannot produce values below −8, since squared pairwise distances cannot exceed 4. If embeddings are unnormalized, vector norms confound the claimed hyperspherical interpretation. The plots and t-SNE visualizations therefore do not yet validate the stronger claim that compression measures semantic well-formedness.

Claims of significant, stable improvements lack repeated-run results or uncertainty estimates. This particularly affects semantic compression: Table 6 reports gains as small as 97.00 to 97.29 on the 700-example SNIPS test set, equivalent to two additional correct predictions, and one configuration does not improve at all. Compression is evaluated quantitatively on only two selected datasets.

The supervision and application scope need clearer qualification. Four datasets supply annotated slots, while nearest-neighbor evaluation uses the full labeled training set. This supports representation learning without intent-label training, but does not demonstrate the stated low-annotation motivation. The source of test-time templates for compression, including whether they use gold annotations or predicted slots, also needs to be explicit.

The broader claims exceed the demonstrated contribution. Experiments cover English intent classification with a limited baseline set; closely related entity-aware approaches are discussed but not compared experimentally. The evidence supports a promising template-based method, but the unresolved objective, evaluation, and reproducibility issues require substantive revision before a Findings recommendation.
